# Blair Thornton of Bachman-Turner Overdrive Celebrates 76th Birthday with Rock Legacy Fans of '70s rock have a reason to celebrate\. Blair Thornton, the guitarist and songwriter best known for his years with Bachman-Turner Overdrive, turns 76 on July 23\. Born in Vancouver, British Columbia, in 1950, Thornton became part of the Canadian rock group's most successful lineup and helped create music that remains beloved well beyond the 1970s\. Before BTO, Thornton played with the British Columbia group Crosstown Bus\. His biggest opportunity came in early 1974 when he replaced founding guitarist Tim Bachman during the tour behind *Bachman-Turner Overdrive II*, joining Randy Bachman, Fred Turner and Robbie Bachman\. Thornton's arrival gave Randy Bachman another skilled lead guitarist to work alongside\. The two could trade parts and play twin-guitar leads, opening up new possibilities for the band as it prepared its next record\. Thornton also contributed backing vocals and quickly became involved in the songwriting\. His first BTO album, *Not Fragile*, arrived later that year and became the band's biggest release\. # Pepper Keenan on the time he got to play Malcolm Young’s legendary AC/DC guitar rig: “It scared the crap out of me\. There’s no overdrive – it’s just volume” Pepper Keenan and Malcolm Young\. Pepper Keenan has looked back on the time he was given the keys to Malcolm Young’s legendary AC/DC rig – an experience he describes as “concussive”\. Speaking on the latest episode of Chris Garza’s podcast, the Corrosion of Conformity guitarist explained the opportunity arose because he and Young both had the same guitar tech, Takumi Suetsugu\. The world-renowned technician, who also worked with Prince, was a mutual contact that connected Keenan’s world of heavy metal with the classic rock style championed by the Young brothers\. As such, Keenan was invited to an AC/DC show by Suetsugu, and offered the chance to play the late rhythm guitar great’s iconic ‘Beast’ Gretsch through his fully fledged stock of Marshall stacks\. Loud is an understatement\. Ear-splitting would be more appropriate\. Keenan compared the experience to getting a concussion\. “\[Suetsugu\] ended up working for AC/DC, and that’s when he called me up\. I went to a show and, yes, I got to play Malcolm’s rig,” he remembers\.
